failures.title: Audi CJSA Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Timing Chain Tensioner Failure - 2012-2016 models
items.whatHappens: The EA111 1.4 TFSI uses a timing chain driven by a hydraulic tensioner that is prone to premature wear. As the tensioner loses pressure, the chain stretches and begins to rattle on cold starts. If left unaddressed, the chain can skip a tooth, causing the pistons to contact the valves and resulting in catastrophic internal damage.
items.repairVsReplace: A standalone timing chain and tensioner kit replacement costs approximately £800-£1,500 and is viable if caught early. If the chain has already jumped or bent valves, a full Audi CJSA engine replacement is the only reliable solution. Read our full timing chain failure guide.

items.title: Carbon Buildup on Intake Valves - All CJSA variants
items.whatHappens: As a direct-injection engine, the CJSA has no fuel washing over the intake valves. Over time, carbon deposits accumulate on the valve stems and ports, restricting airflow. Symptoms include rough idle, hesitation under acceleration, and gradual power loss.
items.repairVsReplace: A walnut blast or chemical intake clean resolves this without engine removal. It does not warrant a full CJSA replacement unless accompanied by valve seat damage from prolonged neglect. Read our full carbon buildup guide.

failures.goodYearsLine: The CJSA was produced throughout the EA111 lifecycle. Post-2016, Audi transitioned to the EA211 belt-driven family (CZDA), which eliminated the timing chain issue entirely. If your CJSA has already had the chain and tensioner replaced with the updated parts, the engine is significantly more reliable going forward .

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the CJSA
variants.intro: The Audi CJSA engine code is stamped directly onto the engine block, typically on a machined pad near the junction of the engine and the transmission bell housing. It is also clearly listed on your V5C registration document under "Engine Number" and can be decoded from your 17-digit VIN.

relatives.description: - The earlier EA111 1.4 TFSI 122hp variant that the CJSA directly succeeded, sharing the same chain-driven architecture and similar coking vulnerabilities.
- The EA211 1.4 TSI that replaced the CJSA, featuring a belt-driven timing system that entirely eliminated the notorious chain tensioner failure risk of the EA111 generation.
The identical physical engine architecture fitted to contemporary Volkswagen Golf and Polo models, sharing the exact same timing chain and carbon buildup failure patterns.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement Audi CJSA - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used Audi CJSA engine is a viable option only if it comes with verifiable proof that the timing chain and tensioner have already been replaced with the updated revision. Without this documentation, you risk inheriting a stretched chain that could fail within thousands of miles of installation. Explore vetted options via our used engines network.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A properly reconditioned CJSA is the recommended choice for most owners. A reputable rebuild will include a new timing chain kit with the revised tensioner, walnut-blasted intake valves, and a verified turbocharger, directly addressing the EA111's known weak points and restoring the engine to reliable operation. Compare reconditioned engines today.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for CJSA units that have suffered secondary damage, such as a jumped timing chain bending valves or scoring cylinder walls. An upgraded rebuild should include new piston rings, a skimmed cylinder head, and the updated chain tensioner to prevent recurrence. Learn more about rebuilt engines.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Opting for a supply-and-fit service through our network ensures the replacement is performed by Audi specialists, with the warranty backed by the installing garage for complete peace of mind. View our supply and fit options.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The CJSA is typically found in Audi A3 (8V) and A1 (8X) models valued between £4,000 and £12,000 . For most examples, a reconditioned engine at £2,000+ remains well within the vehicle's value. However, for sub-£4,000 A1s with high mileage, the replacement cost may approach 50% or more of the vehicle's current market value - evaluate carefully before committing.

mainEntity.name: How much does an Audi CJSA engine replacement cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A reconditioned Audi CJSA engine typically costs between £2,000 and £3,500 for supply-only . Used units start around £800 but carry high risks of undocumented timing chain wear. Fully rebuilt options range from £3,000 to £4,500. Independent fitting labour adds approximately £455-£650 to the total.

mainEntity.name: What is the most common failure with the CJSA engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most frequent documented issue with the Audi CJSA is timing chain tensioner failure, often accompanied by carbon buildup on the intake valves. The hydraulic tensioner can lose pressure, leading to chain stretch and a distinct cold-start rattle. If ignored, the chain can skip a tooth, causing catastrophic valve-to-piston contact.

mainEntity.name: Which Audi models use the CJSA engine code?

acceptedAnswer.text: The CJSA is fitted to mainstream Audi compact models from 2012 to 2016, most notably the A3 (8V) and A1 (8X). It was a high-volume application before Audi transitioned to the belt-driven EA211 engine family. Always verify your specific fitment using your registration number before ordering parts.

mainEntity.name: Should I buy a used or reconditioned CJSA engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: A reconditioned Audi CJSA is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the known risks of inheriting a stretched timing chain. Used engines carry a 3-6 month warranty and may have undocumented tensioner wear. Reconditioned units include a revised timing chain kit with the updated tensioner and a 12-24 month warranty.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my car has the CJSA engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: The CJSA engine code is stamped on a machined pad on the engine block, near the transmission bell housing, and is listed on your V5C registration document. It is commonly confused with the earlier CAXA or the later belt-driven CZDA variants. Fitting the wrong revision can cause ECU mapping mismatches and wiring loom incompatibilities.
